analysis.one_liner: Caps monthly drug copayments at $10 for the lowest-income Medicare beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2006 with no cosponsors and never advanced past committee before Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have capped what the poorest Medicare beneficiaries pay out of pocket for prescription drugs at $10 a month, with the cap rising with inflation each year. It applied to people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid (dual eligibles) and other very-low-income beneficiaries, a group that under the Medicare drug program pays copayments on top of limited incomes. The bill was referred to two House committees and died there when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, roughly the lowest-income Medicare beneficiaries — people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid and other beneficiaries at the lowest income level — would have paid at most $10 per month in drug copayments, protecting fixed-income seniors and disabled beneficiaries from out-of-pocket drug costs that can grow with each prescription.

how_it_helps.text: Caps total copayments for covered Medicare Part D drugs at $10 per month for full-benefit dual eligibles and other lowest-income individuals.
Adjusts the $10 cap upward each year by the consumer price increase, so the protection does not erode over time.
Takes effect for benefits in years after enactment, meaning relief would begin as soon as plans' benefit designs could implement it.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare prescription drug plans and, ultimately, federal taxpayers would absorb the cost of copayments above $10 a month that the plans would no longer collect from the lowest-income enrollees; the plans' monthly premium subsidies or bids would need to reflect that added cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill contained no dedicated funding source in its text; capping copayments would shift costs to drug plans and the federal government, raising program costs that could flow into premiums paid by all beneficiaries and taxpayers.

A flat monthly cap is blunt: it helps enrollees with many prescriptions the most but does nothing to lower the underlying list prices of drugs, and it does nothing for low-income beneficiaries who fall just above the eligibility line.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: a $10 monthly cap gives the poorest Medicare beneficiaries predictable, bounded drug costs, which is a straightforward hardship relief. The costs — higher plan bids and federal spending — are real but modest relative to the population covered, and indexing the cap keeps it meaningful. The bill was a one-page policy with no revenue offset, so an honest supporter would acknowledge it raised program costs without identifying how to pay for them, but its design flaws are minor compared with the protection it offered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final month of the two-year Congress, referred to two committees that never acted on it, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Crowley introduced the bill on December 5, 2006, in the final month of the 109th Congress.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee; neither committee took it up.
Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill died with it, never receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare prescription drug plans were better off, because they never had to absorb copayment costs above $10 a month for their lowest-income enrollees; the lowest-income beneficiaries gained nothing, as their copayments stayed as they were.

for.name: Rep. Joseph Crowley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only supporter in Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over Medicare Part D
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support was a single Democrat, and no Republican cosponsored or acted on it before it expired.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plans (private insurers)
industries.note: The bill would have stopped these plans from collecting copayments above $10 a month from their lowest-income enrollees, requiring plans to absorb that cost or bill the federal program instead. The plans' interest in the bill ran against the beneficiaries it protected, since their revenue from cost-sharing would be capped.

By lowering out-of-pocket costs for the poorest beneficiaries, the cap would remove a barrier to filling prescriptions, potentially increasing drug purchases. Manufacturers would gain volume while the cost of the cap fell on plans and the government, not on drug prices.
